title: NAB back pays $170m in massive payroll failure
full_text:
National Australia Bank has agreed to back pay $169 million to tens of thousands of staff after underpaying them for more than a decade by failing to record their actual hours of work and under-resourcing its payroll teams, failures that led the board to cut executive bonuses by up to 30 per cent.
NAB will pay a record $2 million contrition payment for errors that date back to 2012 as part of an enforceable undertaking with the Fair Work Ombudsman that also commits the bank’s executives to start early compliance planning for any new enterprise agreement – a first for such an undertaking.
The underpayments totalling $127 million without interest and superannuation and affecting 66,000 workers across the country represent the biggest wage shortfall in the banking industry so far.
Staff were underpaid minimum award wages, penalty rates, shift loadings, overtime, allowances, termination payments, annual, personal and long service leave, and superannuation.
Many of the underpayments were the result of the bank failing to reconcile workers’ salaries with their actual hours worked, which resulted in some employees’ hourly pay falling below the award minimum.
Average back pay was about $1934 but ranged from less than $5 to more than $87,000.
NAB’s group executive of people and culture, Sarah White, said the bank took its payroll obligations “extremely seriously” as a basic element in employing people.
“We sincerely apologise for these unintended errors. We have and will continue to remediate anyone who has been impacted,” she said.
The Finance Sector Union described the NAB underpayment as a “systemic failure” and “one of the worst cases of employee ‘underpayment’ in Australian corporate history”.
“This was not an accident or a one off, the bank knew there was an issue and didn’t act – NAB executives must be held accountable for that,” FSU national president Wendy Streets said.
Last week NAB’s annual report revealed the board had cut the bonuses of two executives by between 5 and 30 per cent, or about $360,000 in total, due to “accountability for the issues contributing to NAB’s payroll remediation”.
The FWO and payroll experts have been raising the alarm about major corporates’ lax approach to wage compliance and underfunding payroll teams for the past decade.
While NAB paid $2 million for the errors, the informal penalty is a fraction of the Federal Court’s $10 million fine to Commonwealth Bank for failing to do regular audits or compliance checks for just 7400 salaried staff.
Fair Work Ombudsman Anna Booth said an enforceable undertaking was appropriate as NAB had co-operated with the FWO’s investigation and agreed to fully back pay staff outside the six-year limitation period.
“It’s particularly disappointing to see these types of large and long-running underpayment issues in such a well-resourced employer, including where it negotiated its own legally enforceable enterprise agreement terms but failed to make sure it had in place fully compliant payroll systems capable of giving effect to those terms before they became operational,” she said.
Booth highlighted the bank had committed to reforms, including a steering committee chaired by the people and culture executive, as well as an executive review of the payroll program and systems to inform the board of non-compliance.
NAB first self-reported underpayments to the FWO in 2019 after realising it had made significant errors in implementing its most recent enterprise agreement, prompting it to conduct a broad review dating back to 2012.
Despite this, five years later in 2024, NAB realised it had again underpaid staff by not properly addressing non-compliance issues.
The FWO said the underlying causes included NAB’s deficient governance and compliance oversights, inadequate record-keeping, legacy payroll technology, and “limited investment in specialist capability relevant to payroll operations”.
As a result, NAB did not do regular reconciliation checks on staff’s wages – which were required by its agreement – and failed to pay any shortfalls that arose when comparing what staff would have earned under the award.
Other basic failings, identified by the FWO, included NAB not adequately capturing staff’s time and attendance, not accruing staff leave correctly, and either misapplying or not applying at all entitlements under successive enterprise agreements.
The bank has already rectified the majority of underpayments, from 2012 to 2016, and back paid $155 million to current and former employees, including $25 million in interest and $8 million in superannuation.
Westpac admitted last year to underpaying 47,000 staff by $50.2 million over 11 years. The bank paid an $800,000 contrition payment to the Commonwealth.
This followed a previous underpayment in 2020 of $8 million in long service leave entitlements.
In recent years, Westpac brought back timesheets for salaried staff earning up to $140,000 a year to ensure it recorded actual hours worked.
